title: Episode 332: George V: The House of Windsor, the Trenches of the Western Front, the General Strike, and the Royal Christmas Broadcast
description:
The steady, duty-bound twenty-five-year reign of King George V, the sovereign who guided Britain through the most turbulent quarter-century in modern history. Trained as a naval officer, George succeeded in 1910 amidst constitutional deadlock. When World War I shattered European civilization in 1914, George made four hundred visits to frontline troops and hospitals, relinquishing all German titles in 1917 to rebrand the royal family as the House of Windsor. Navigating the 1926 General Strike and appointing Britain's first Labour government, George pioneered modern royal broadcasting with his iconic 1932 Christmas message, cementing the modern constitutional monarchy. Discover the founder of the House of Windsor.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series examines the sovereign who steered Britain through the horrors of the Great War, founded the House of Windsor, and created the modern royal broadcast: King George V. Here is George with the magnificent story of the King who guided Britain through the storm.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE RELUCTANT SAILOR PRINCE: 1865 TO 1910
Born in June 1865 at Marlborough House, Prince George was the second son of the Prince of Wales. Never expecting to inherit the throne, George was educated aboard the naval training ship HMS Britannia alongside his older brother Prince Albert Victor ('Eddy'). George spent fourteen years as a professional naval officer, commanding torpedo boats and gunboats, developing a lifelong devotion to naval punctuality, neatness, and blunt, straightforward honesty. But in January 1892, his elder brother Eddy died suddenly of pneumonia during an influenza epidemic. George was thrust into the direct line of succession. In May 1893, George married Eddy's grieving fiancée, Princess Mary of Teck—affectionately known as 'May'—a woman of formidable dignity, intelligence, and moral strength. Their marriage was a profoundly happy, devoted partnership. Ascending the throne in May 1910 at age forty-four, George was unassuming, conservative, loved stamp collecting, and was famously described as having no personal vices except smoking and shooting pheasants. Prince George had spent fourteen happy years as a career naval officer in the Royal Navy, commanding gunboats and torpedo craft across the Mediterranean and Caribbean. He had never expected or desired to be king until the sudden, tragic death of his elder brother, Prince Albert Victor ('Eddy'), from pneumonia in 1892 thrust George into the direct line of succession. George dutifully married Eddy's fiancee, Princess Victoria Mary of Teck—affectionately known as 'May'—and together they forged one of the most steadfast, devoted marriages in royal history. George lived a simple, methodical country life at York Cottage on the Sandringham estate, setting his clocks half an hour fast, strictly cataloging his world-renowned stamp collection, and avoiding all metropolitan glamour, embodying the quiet, reliable virtues of the British middle class.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE CONSTITUTIONAL SETTLEMENT AND THE DELHI DURBAR: 1910 TO 1911
George's reign began in the crucible of constitutional crisis: the battle over the House of Lords. Following two general elections in 1910, King George gave his reluctant, secret guarantee to Prime Minister Asquith to create enough Liberal peers to pass the Parliament Act if the Lords rejected it. Faced with royal creation, the Tory peers surrendered in August 1911, passing the Parliament Act, which permanently ended the Lords' power to veto legislation. In December 1911, George V made history by traveling to India for the Imperial Delhi Durbar—the only British monarch ever to visit India while on the throne. Wearing the Imperial Crown of India adorned with six thousand diamonds, emeralds, and rubies, George sat upon a golden throne before a crowd of five hundred thousand cheering Indian subjects, dramatically announcing the transfer of the capital of India from Calcutta to New Delhi, cementing the imperial bond. King George V's fortitude during the Parliament Act crisis of 1911 established his credentials as a scrupulous constitutional monarch. Facing relentless pressure from Prime Minister Asquith, George reluctantly agreed to create enough peers to pass the reform bill if the House of Lords persisted in its defiance. When the conservative peers capitulated, the Parliament Act of 1911 permanently stripped the House of Lords of its veto power over financial legislation. Later that year, George and Queen Mary traveled to India for the magnificent Delhi Durbar, becoming the only British sovereign and empress to appear before their Indian subjects in person. Dressed in royal robes and wearing the Imperial Crown of India, George addressed an assembled multitude of over one hundred thousand people, projecting majestic imperial continuity.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE CRUCIBLE OF THE GREAT WAR: 1914 TO 1918
In August 1914, the catastrophe of the First World War engulfed Europe. King George threw himself into the war effort with unflagging, tireless devotion: he made four hundred and fifty visits to military hospitals, inspected thousands of factories and shipyards, and made seven dangerous visits to the frontline trenches in France and Belgium, riding within range of German artillery. In October 1915, during an inspection of troops in France, his horse was frightened by cheering soldiers, reared, and fell backwards on top of the King, crushing his pelvis and leaving him in severe pain for the rest of his life. To set an example of national sacrifice, George instituted 'the King's Pledge', banishing all alcohol from the royal household for the duration of the war, and insisted on strict wartime food rationing at Buckingham Palace. During the grueling four years of the First World War, King George V became the tireless father figure of the British nation. He made over four hundred visits to military hospitals, personally pinned decorations onto thousands of wounded soldiers, and visited the muddy trenches of the Western Front seven times to inspect his troops under enemy shellfire. In 1915, while reviewing troops in France, his horse was startled by cheering soldiers and reared, throwing the King and falling heavily upon him, fracturing his pelvis and causing chronic pain that plagued him for the rest of his life. Despite his injuries, George never rested, embodying unshakeable British resolve through the darkest hours of the Somme, Passchendaele, and the German Spring Offensive.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE CREATION OF THE HOUSE OF WINDSOR: JULY 1917
By 1917, as the Russian Revolution toppled King George's cousin Tsar Nicholas II and German Gotha bombers dropped bombs on London schools, public anti-German sentiment reached fever pitch. H. G. Wells published an article criticizing the British court as 'alien and uninspiring'. King George famously retorted with unvarnished fury: 'I may be uninspiring, but I'll be damned if I'm an alien!' On July 17, 1917, George issued a historic royal proclamation: he relinquished all German titles, degrees, and dignities, declaring that henceforth the British royal family and all descendants of Queen Victoria would bear the purely English name of the House of Windsor, taken from his ancestral royal castle. Simultaneously, his Battenberg cousins anglicized their name to Mountbatten. When Kaiser Wilhelm II heard the news in Germany, he remarked sarcastically that he looked forward to seeing a performance of Shakespeare's comedy 'The Merry Wives of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha'. The historic renaming of the royal house in July 1917 was a masterstroke of political survival. With anti-German sentiment at fever pitch as London suffered bombings by German Gotha aircraft, the King recognized that the German family name of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha was a dangerous liability. Working with his private secretary, Lord Stamfordham, the King searched British history for an inspiring name, rejecting Plantagenet and Tudor before settling on 'Windsor', after the ancient fortress that had sheltered British monarchs since William the Conqueror. George simultaneously relinquished all German titles, orders, and honors held by his family, commanding his royal relatives to adopt English surnames like Mountbatten and Cambridge, thoroughly nationalizing the British monarchy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: SURVIVING REVOLUTION: THE GENERAL STRIKE AND THE FIRST LABOUR GOVERNMENT: 1924 TO 1926
While monarchies collapsed across Russia, Germany, Austria-Hungary, and the Ottoman Empire in the aftermath of the war, King George V preserved the British Crown through unmatched constitutional impartiality and deep working-class empathy. In January 1924, when the Conservatives were defeated, George invited Ramsay MacDonald to form Britain's first-ever socialist Labour government. While aristocratic courtiers panicked, George treated MacDonald and his working-class ministers with absolute courtesy, remarking in his diary: 'Today, 23 years to the day since dear Grandmamma died, I have associated with the Labour Party... I think they are reasonable men.' During the nine-day General Strike of May 1926, when millions of workers walked out and Tory politicians called the strikers revolutionaries, King George intervened firmly to urge conciliation, rebuking a wealthy coal owner with the memorable words: 'Try living on their wages before you judge them!' In January 1924, King George V faced a momentous constitutional test when Ramsay MacDonald formed Britain's first-ever Labour government. While nervous aristocratic courtiers feared that socialist revolutionaries had seized control of the British state, George received MacDonald and his working-class ministers at Buckingham Palace with genuine warmth, courtesy, and respect. George worked constructively with the Labour leadership, assuring them: 'You will find me always ready to help you.' During the 1926 General Strike, when millions of workers downed tools and Winston Churchill urged aggressive military suppression, the King urged calm and reconciliation, protecting Britain from the violent social upheavals that tore continental Europe apart.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE WIRELESS AND THE CHRISTMAS BROADCAST OF 1932
In 1932, King George pioneered an invention that would forever redefine the relationship between the British sovereign and people: the radio broadcast. Encouraged by BBC founding Director-General John Reith, George agreed to deliver the first royal Christmas broadcast on December 25, 1932, from a small temporary studio at Sandringham. The text, written for the King by poet Rudyard Kipling, began with the immortal words: 'I speak now from my home and from my heart to you all; to men and women so cut off by the snows, the desert, or the sea, that only voices out of the air can reach them.' Broadcast live across the British Empire to twenty million listeners, the King's warm, fatherly voice brought the royal family directly into the living rooms of ordinary citizens, establishing an annual holiday tradition that endures to this day. The 1932 Christmas broadcast was a landmark cultural moment that brought the monarch directly into the homes of millions. Written by the celebrated poet and novelist Rudyard Kipling, the broadcast began with the King's gravelly, resonant voice echoing through radio sets across six continents: 'I speak now from my home and my heart to you all; to men and women so cut off by the snows, the desert, or the sea, that only voices out of the air can reach them.' The direct, intimate medium transformed the King from an aloof, distant imperial figure into a beloved, benevolent father of a worldwide family of nations, solidifying the emotional foundations of the modern Commonwealth of Nations.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE SILVER JUBILEE AND THE PEACEFUL PASSING: 1935 TO 1936
In May 1935, Great Britain celebrated King George V's Silver Jubilee, marking twenty-five years on the throne. As the King and Queen Mary rode through the poor, working-class streets of the East End of London, crowds greeted them with ecstatic, thunderous cheers, hanging homemade bunting between tenements. The modest King was deeply moved, recording in his diary: 'I'd no idea they felt like that about me. I am beginning to think they must really like me for myself.' Yet George was tormented by anxiety over his eldest son, David, Prince of Wales, predicting with chilling accuracy: 'After I am dead, the boy will ruin himself in twelve months.' In January 1936, seventy-year-old King George lay dying of chronic bronchitis at Sandringham. On the night of January 20, 1936, his physician, Lord Dawson of Penn, administered a lethal injection of morphine and cocaine to ensure the King died peacefully before midnight, so that his death would be announced in the dignified morning editions of The Times rather than the vulgar evening papers. George V died at eleven fifty-five at night. He had preserved the British monarchy through the greatest convulsions of modern history, establishing the House of Windsor as the enduring anchor of the British nation. In May 1935, King George V's Silver Jubilee brought millions of cheering citizens into the streets of London, stunning the modest old King. Surprised by the immense outpouring of popular affection, George remarked humbly: 'I am beginning to think they must really like me for myself.' Yet his final months were overshadowed by deep anxiety over his eldest son, the Prince of Wales, whom George foresaw would ruin the monarchy over Mrs. Wallis Simpson. George prophetically declared: 'After I am dead, the boy will ruin himself within twelve months.' When King George V died peacefully at Sandringham on January 20, 1936, his doctor, Lord Dawson of Penn, administered a lethal dose of morphine and cocaine to ensure the King's death could be announced in the morning edition of The Times. George V left behind a beloved, resilient monarchy that had survived war, depression, and empire.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for joining us for this episode of Most Fascinating Stories. Until next time, I'm Rebecca.
